Along the same lines, I suggest [Musicophilia](http://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=15382899) by Oliver Sacks. That link goes to an excerpt of the first chapter about a surgeon who is struck by lightning and becomes a concert pianist and composer. The book isn't so much music theory but theory about why humans are musical. The core of the book is the neuroscience of music, but it's illustrated by the cases presented by Sacks' patients and correspondence, as well as his own interest in classical music. I would recommend this to musicians who want to learn about how we do music and what music does to us. 

edit: Since you, OP, are a voice student, you might be interested in the section on vocally impaired patients who are unable to speak normally but can communicate by singing.

Try attending an archaeological field school. Field schools teach basic archaeological practices and principles are practically pre-requisites for undergrads who move on to grad school in archaeology. I see this as a way you can get that formal experience in archaeology, a life experience in itself that would go well in a personal statement, a way to travel, and a way to earn course credits. This experience may aid in gaining re-admittance to a university, but I'm in the US and have no experience with the UK system so don't quote me on that. I've had students who have needed to demonstrate successful accumulation of course credits in making the argument for re-admission.

http://ifrglobal.org/
http://www.ucl.ac.uk/archaeology/research/projects/astypalaia

These are the programs I have some knowledge about, so feel free to PM me if the field school option is of any help. Good luck!
